body:
Copying, comparing, serializing, hashing, merging, diffing, converting and
destroying a value, and the CBOR, MessagePack, UBJSON, BJData and BON8 writers
recurse a fixed number of nesting levels on the call stack and finish deeper
levels with an explicit stack (#5387). The number was hard-coded to 128. That is
too much for small stacks: a 128-level dump() needs about 288 KiB at -O0 with
Clang (2.3 KiB per level; 256 KiB with GCC) and crashed in a thread with a
256 KiB stack, and musl threads have 128 KiB by default. Others may want the
opposite.

The macro JSON_RECURSION_DEPTH_LIMIT, defined before including the library,
sets the number; the default stays 128. The value must be an integer constant
from 0 to 254 (not a floating-point number or bool), otherwise a static_assert
names the macro. 254 is the largest value because the copy constructor and the
comparison operators cannot pass a depth down and count it in a byte per thread
(nesting_depth()). The guard that counts now counts only the levels it enters,
so the count never exceeds the limit. It used to count the level that finds the
limit reached as well, which made the count 255 at limit 254: a copy made by a
custom base class while a copy was going on then wrapped the byte to 0 and
recursed another 254 levels (twice the stack).

0 is allowed: every walk then uses its explicit stack from the first level on
and needs a constant amount of stack (16 KiB or less at
-O0 with Clang and GCC, for a value nested 20,000 levels deep). All uses of the
limit compare a depth with it; none computes limit - 1 or limit + 1, and no
walk has a constant 128 of its own.

The macro changes only stack use and speed, never a result. Like
JSON_NO_THREAD_LOCAL it is not part of the ABI tag and must be the same in all
translation units (ODR); the page of the macro says what happens otherwise.

Supporting a limit of 0 needed one fix: update() without merge_objects reached
the explicit-stack merge at depth 0, which always merges objects. update_members
now takes that path only with merge_objects, which is the only case in which it
recurses at all.

Measurements (macOS arm64, Apple clang 21 and g++ 16, documented in the macro
page with a table per operation and optimization level, and a program to
reproduce them): the stack needed at the default of 128 levels is up to 288 KiB
(dump at -O0, Clang), 224 KiB (copy), and 48 KiB or less at -O2; at 254 levels
up to 576 KiB at -O0 and 112 KiB at -O2. Speed at -O2 relative to the default:
ordinary documents (nested 2 to 10 levels) are 1.1 to 2.4 times as slow with a
limit of 0 or 1 and unchanged (within about 0.1) with 16 or 254; values nested
1,000 or 100,000 levels deep show no difference for any limit. The default
build does the same work as before: the instructions retired for copy and conversion
(the walks whose guard changed; net of loading, canada, citm, twitter, jeopardy
and deep values), ==, dump and hash differ from the base by at most 0.02 % for copy
and 0.71 % in either direction for the others (noise), and the cycles for copy
by at most 0.65 %.

Tests: the existing tests that depended on 128 (comparison, allocator, custom
base class, diagnostics, binary writers, patch, merge_diff, conversions, custom
array type) derive their depths from the limit, and two assumed a limit of at
least 1 (limit - 1 wrapped around). tests/src/unit-recursion_depth_limit.cpp
checks that the macro is honoured (the array type of a value counts the levels
that a copy and a comparison descend) and that all walks return the same results
for values nested 1 to 300 levels deep as arrays, objects and both, against
expected strings and bytes built independently of the library; CMake builds it
with limits 0, 1 and 254 besides the default, and the CI target
ci_test_recursion_depth_limit_0 runs the whole suite with a limit of 0. A test
with a base class that copies the value from its copy constructor covers the
wrap-around at 254. The new test does not compile against the
previous header with -DJSON_RECURSION_DEPTH_LIMIT=1.

Docs: new macro page (range, stack and speed tables, small-stack guidance, ODR),
index, nav, macro overview, "Nesting depth" of the untrusted-input page (which
claimed that no walk could exhaust the stack however deep a value is nested; the
default assumes a stack of a few hundred KiB), the assurance case, and the page
of JSON_NO_THREAD_LOCAL.



## Breaking changes

No breaking changes: the default stays 128, and the macro is new. Like `JSON_NO_THREAD_LOCAL` it is not part of the ABI tag and must be the same in all translation units; the macro page says what happens otherwise.

review_comments.body: I would hope that this gets optimized to a simple return.  Should it be put in a `constexpr std::size_t depth_limit` to be sure?
review_comments.diff_hunk:
@@ -20,21 +33,59 @@ namespace detail
 @brief the number of nesting levels an operation recurses into
 
 Operations that walk a value (copying, comparing, serializing, hashing, merging,
-...) recurse once
-per nesting level, which is fastest, but a value nested deeply enough would
-exhaust the call stack. So they recurse only this many levels deep and finish
-whatever lies below with an explicit stack. All of them share this limit.
+diffing, converting, destroying, and writing the binary formats CBOR,
+MessagePack, UBJSON, BJData, and BON8) recurse once per nesting level, which is
+fastest, but a value nested deeply enough would exhaust the call stack. So they
+recurse only this many levels deep and finish whatever lies below with an
+explicit stack that lives on the heap. All of them share this limit and none has
+a constant of its own. It is the value of the macro JSON_RECURSION_DEPTH_LIMIT,
+128 by default. (Parsing, the binary readers, flatten(), unflatten(), and
+to_bson() always use an explicit stack and do not read it, and the lockstep
+comparison of json_view documents has a fixed bound of its own, 48 levels.)
+
+Most of the operations pass the depth down as an argument. The copy constructor
+and the comparison operators cannot, as their signatures are fixed, so they
+count it in basic_json::nesting_depth() instead, a byte per thread. Only the
+levels that are descended into are counted, so the count never exceeds the limit.
+The limit must fit in the byte with some headroom, so that the count cannot wrap
+around: it must be below 255, and 254 is the largest value allowed. (More levels
+would hardly be useful: 254 levels need up to 576 KiB of stack in an unoptimized
+build already, twice the stack of the default.)
+
+The smallest value is 0: every operation then uses its explicit stack from the
+first level on and no operation recurses over the nesting of a value at all.
+That is slower, but needs a constant amount of call stack. It works because
+every use of the limit compares a depth with it (`depth >= limit`, or `<` for
+the opposite), which holds for 0 as for any other value; nothing computes
+`limit - 1` or `limit + 1`, so nothing wraps around. Each operation's explicit
+stack handles any nesting level, including the first, so none of them relies on
+having recursed first.
 
-Most of them pass the depth down as an argument. The copy constructor and the
-comparison operators cannot, as their signatures are fixed, so they count it
-in basic_json::nesting_depth() instead, a byte per thread; the limit must
-therefore stay below 255.
+The call stack that an operation needs is roughly a few KiB plus a cost per level
+times the limit. At the default of 128 levels, an unoptimized build needs up to
+about 290 KiB (`dump()` with Clang at -O0: about 2.3 KiB per level) and an
+optimized build up to about 48 KiB; with 254 levels it is up to 576 KiB and
+112 KiB, and with 0 it is 16 KiB or less. Lower the limit for threads with small
+stacks (RTOS tasks, fibers, musl threads), raise it to trade stack for speed on
+deeply nested values. All of this, with the measurements, is in the
+documentation of the macro.
 
+@sa https://json.nlohmann.me/api/macros/json_recursion_depth_limit/
 @sa https://github.com/nlohmann/json/issues/5387
 */
 constexpr std::size_t recursion_depth_limit() noexcept
 {
-    return 128;
+    // an integer: not a floating-point number, whose range check would pass for 1.5 or 254.0
+    // (bool is an integer type, too, but 1 and 0 spelled true and false are no way to say a limit)
+    static_assert(std::is_integral<decltype(JSON_RECURSION_DEPTH_LIMIT)>::value
+                  && !std::is_same<decltype(JSON_RECURSION_DEPTH_LIMIT), bool>::value,
+                  "JSON_RECURSION_DEPTH_LIMIT must be an integer constant");
+    static_assert(JSON_RECURSION_DEPTH_LIMIT >= 0 && JSON_RECURSION_DEPTH_LIMIT <= 254,
+                  "JSON_RECURSION_DEPTH_LIMIT must be between 0 and 254: the nesting depth is counted in a byte per thread "
+                  "and may exceed the limit by one (see https://json.nlohmann.me/api/macros/json_recursion_depth_limit/)");
+    // (a value out of range has been reported by now; the remainder keeps it
+    // below 255 for any value, so that basic_json does not report it again)
+    return static_cast<std::size_t>(JSON_RECURSION_DEPTH_LIMIT) % 255;

review_comments.body: Is this needed now that there are static asserts in `recursion_depth_limit.hpp`?  I suppose it doesn't hurt either way.
review_comments.diff_hunk:
@@ -1256,8 +1256,12 @@ class basic_json // NOLINT(cppcoreguidelines-special-member-functions,hicpp-spec
     }
 
 #ifndef JSON_NO_THREAD_LOCAL
-    // nesting_depth() is a byte and may exceed the limit by one level
-    static_assert(detail::recursion_depth_limit() < 255, "the nesting depth count must fit in a byte");
+    // nesting_depth() is a byte that never exceeds the limit (JSON_RECURSION_DEPTH_LIMIT),
+    // which is at most 254: the largest value stays one below the byte's maximum, so
+    // that the count cannot wrap around to 0 and let a descent go on without a bound.
+    // (recursion_depth_limit() checks the macro itself, with a message that
+    // names it; this is the check that cannot be edited away unnoticed.)
+    static_assert(detail::recursion_depth_limit() < 255, "the nesting depth count must fit in a byte: JSON_RECURSION_DEPTH_LIMIT must not exceed 254");

review_comments.body:
It already is a simple return: `recursion_depth_limit()` is `constexpr`, so the value is computed at compile time even at -O0 (the function body is `mov x0, #128; ret`), and from -O1 on Clang and GCC 16 inline the call into `cmp x0, #127`. Only an unoptimized build keeps the call, so I kept the function, which predates this PR and has about 20 callers. With the redundant `static_assert` in `json.hpp` removed in `e3940d20b7`, the `% 255` is gone as well, and the function is a plain `return static_cast<std::size_t>(JSON_RECURSION_DEPTH_LIMIT);`.

*(Written by Claude Code on behalf of @nlohmann.)*

review_comments.body:
Right: it was not needed. Because of the `% 255`, `recursion_depth_limit()` could never return 255 or more, so this assert could never fire. The remainder only existed to keep it from reporting the same error a second time. Fixed in `e3940d20b7`: both are removed, and the comment at `nesting_depth()` now points to the range check in `recursion_depth_limit()`. Defining the macro as 255, -1, 1000, 1.5 or `true` still gives exactly one error naming `JSON_RECURSION_DEPTH_LIMIT` (checked with Clang and GCC 16).

*(Written by Claude Code on behalf of @nlohmann.)*

Right, that is already handled: there is nothing to compute per call. `recursion_depth_limit()` is `constexpr` and returns the macro value cast to `std::size_t`, so the result is a compile-time constant, and a `static` local would add nothing (and is not allowed in a C++11 `constexpr` function).

title: Add JSON_RECURSION_DEPTH_LIMIT to set how deep value walks recurse
